paragraphs.text: Loose [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) from Yunnan, made in the 1990s and stored in Guangzhou. It was never pressed into a cake or brick, so air moves freely through the leaf and it ages along a more even path.

The leaf was fermented in a covered [wet pile](shou:wet-piling), a method Yunnan’s state factories brought into production in 1973 to give in weeks what raw pu’er took years to reach. At thirty-one years it is well past the decade that marks [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged), and it keeps changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why storage counts as much as the years.

brewing.text: Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
